summary: TechCrunch explainer on Tesla's Cybertruck after its long-delayed launch, covering the three variants, pricing, range, and availability. It also addresses the steel design, resale rules, bed size, and the climate and safety concerns of large EVs. First deliveries to about 10 high-profile customers took place November 30, 2023 at Tesla's Austin Gigafactory.
one_line: TechCrunch FAQ on Tesla's Cybertruck covering its three variants, prices, delivery timeline, design, resale rules and environmental concerns after the November 2023 launch.
key_facts: The Cybertruck is Tesla's first new model since 2020, when it started delivering the Model Y.
Elon Musk showed an early Cybertruck at a 2019 event, where two windows were accidentally smashed during a durability demo.
First deliveries to about 10 high-profile customers, including Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, occurred November 30 at the Tesla Gigafactory in Austin.
In 2019 Tesla promised a $39,900 single-motor rear-wheel-drive Cybertruck with 250-mile range; the rear-wheel version now starts at $60,990 and won't be available until 2025.
The all-wheel drive Cybertruck has an estimated 340-mile range, a top speed of 112 mph, and a $79,990 starting price.
The Cyberbeast has three motors, 845 horsepower, 0 to 60 mph in 2.6 seconds, a 130 mph top speed, an estimated 320-mile range and a $99,990 price.
The all-wheel drive and Cyberbeast versions both have a claimed towing capacity of 11,000 pounds.
A range extender would push the all-wheel drive to an estimated 470 miles and the Cyberbeast to over 440 miles; Musk said it fits in about 1/3 of the truck bed.
Musk described the Cybertruck as “an armored personnel carrier from the future — what Bladerunner would have driven.”
Tesla expects to mass produce Cybertrucks starting in 2024, and reservations dating to 2019 get priority; some reservations have appeared on eBay for $10,000.
Tesla's November 2023 update to its U.S. order agreement page removed rules that barred resale in the first year and sought $50,000 in damages from early resellers.
Under current rules, trucks and SUVs priced above $80,000 don't qualify for the $7,500 federal EV tax credit.
The production truck bed is six feet and slightly longer with the tailgate down, so a bike will likely need a wheel hanging over the tailgate.
Experts warn that larger, heavier vehicles need more battery materials, raising environmental cost, and are less safe for pedestrians.
